description: I'm a student in Engineering Physics from UFSCar in Brazil, doing in internship in Carleton University. My background includes image processing and computer vision, machine learning applied to predicting biotic and abiotic stress in plants, spectroscopy, optics, and photonics, as well as photonics and machine learning applied to lubricating oil monitoring.
summary:
Soybean farmers in Mato Grosso, Brazil, decide every February what to plant after harvest. The rain window is short, and the choice determines water risk, soil health and pest pressure for the following years. This decision is currently made by experience, without data specific to each field.
Field Shift supports that decision with satellite data. The tool reads each field's NDVI history from NASA MODIS and ESA Sentinel-2 and predicts the soybean harvest date as a P10, P50 and P90 range. This range measures the planting window remaining in the season. The tool then evaluates four succession strategies: second-crop corn, the current practice, corn with brachiaria, sorghum or millet, and a crotalaria cover crop. Each strategy is tested against 26 years of NASA POWER and GPM rainfall in a daily water balance, scored on bare-soil days observed by satellite, and adjusted for slope from SRTM and for pest cycle effects. The farmer sets the weight given to income, soil protection and risk.
The interface is a satellite map of eleven demonstration fields near Sorriso, Mato Grosso, Brazil, with ranked strategy cards per field. It runs in the browser, works on a phone, and states where the data ends and the agronomist's judgment begins.
details:
Brazil harvests the largest soybean crop on Earth, about 180 million tonnes in 2025/26, and the state of Mato Grosso alone produces more than 50 million of them, more than any country except the United States, Argentina and Brazil itself. Almost all of it is rainfed. When the soybean comes off in January and February, the same land immediately hosts Brazil's second-crop corn, the "safrinha", and Mato Grosso again leads with 49% of the national safrinha production. This double-crop system feeds a large share of the world's grain trade, and it hangs on one narrow hinge: the few weeks of rain left between the soybean harvest and the dry season.

Every February, each farmer decides what goes into that window. Sow corn too late and it flowers into drought; repeat corn year after year and the soil spends the dry season bare while nematodes and the corn leafhopper build up. The information needed to decide well exists, but it is scattered: satellites observe every field, decades of rainfall are public, and the agronomic literature is clear about rotation benefits. What is missing is a tool that brings all of it down to the scale where the decision is actually made, the individual field. That is what Field Shift does.

The farmer selects a field on a satellite map. The page shows the predicted harvest window as three dates, P10, P50 and P90: there is a 10% chance the harvest happens before the P10 date, 50% before P50, and 90% before P90. P50 is the expected date, and the interval from P10 to P90 expresses how certain the prediction is. The page also shows the field's NDVI curve with that window marked, and four ranked strategy cards for what to plant after the soybean: second-crop corn, which is the current practice, corn with brachiaria, sorghum or millet, and a crotalaria cover crop. The controls re-rank the cards instantly: a slider for harvest delay, an El Nino and La Nina filter, priority weights for income, soil protection and risk, and checkboxes for constraints such as owning cattle, holding a corn contract, or known pest presence.

The pipeline has four stages, each grounded in published literature, and all code is open source in the repository.

The first stage predicts the harvest. Detecting crop stages from smoothed vegetation-index time series is an established method, with reported errors of 3 to 12 days for rice, maize and soybean (Sakamoto et al., 2005, Remote Sensing of Environment 96:366-374; Sakamoto et al., 2010, RSE 114:2146-2159). For each field, Sentinel-2 (10 m) and MODIS (daily) NDVI from 2019 onward are merged and smoothed with a Savitzky-Golay filter, the standard method for reconstructing NDVI series under cloud contamination (Chen et al., 2004, RSE 91:332-344), and used to detect emergence, peak and harvest dates for every past season. We built a growing-degree-day model on top of this first and discarded it: the thermal requirement implied by NDVI-detected harvests swung too widely between seasons, giving a mean absolute error of 13.7 days in leave-one-season-out replays. The shipped model instead regresses cycle duration on two predictors already available in December, the spring rainfall accumulated from September 1 and the field's emergence day of year, re-centered by each field's own median residual, with P10, P50 and P90 read off the pooled residual distribution. Dry springs and earlier emergence both lengthen the cycle the satellite sees. Replaying the 2025/26 season with all data frozen on December 15, the P50 prediction landed a mean of 4.5 days from the harvest date later detected by satellite across eleven fields: nine fields fell within 5 days, two missed by 11 days, just outside the 10-day tolerance we set for ourselves before looking at the results, and the actual harvest landed inside the P10-P90 window on every field. That error sits inside the 3-to-12-day band the literature reports for this class of method. We kept the tolerance as written rather than widening it after the fact, and the two outliers are an open item in the repository.

The second stage measures climate risk. For each candidate crop, each sowing date from January to March on a 5-day grid, and each year from 2000 to 2026, the tool simulates a daily 100 mm soil water balance: NASA POWER and GPM rainfall in, crop demand out, with reference evapotranspiration derived from radiation and stage coefficients from the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998). This is the same logic Brazil's official climate-risk zoning (ZARC/MAPA) uses to define sowing windows from simulated water balance. A year counts as a failure when water stress during the crop's flowering stage exceeds its tolerance, and the share of successful years is the success probability. The results reproduce the gradient documented in Embrapa's second-crop corn literature, where yield potential falls and drought risk rises as sowing is delayed: in our table, corn sown on January 31 succeeds in 69% of the 27 historical years, drops to 50% by February 5, and reaches zero from February 20 onward, while millet still succeeds in 73% of years sown as late as March 17. That divergence is the whole decision: it is why a ten-day harvest delay can turn the ranking over. The probability is also computed separately for El Nino, La Nina and neutral years classified by the NOAA ONI index, following evidence that ENSO phase changes the length and timing of the sowing window in Central Brazil and that cropping calendars should be adjusted per phase (Heinemann et al., 2021, International Journal of Climatology, doi 10.1002/joc.6684). The interface offers All years, La Nina and El Nino as filters; the neutral sample is only five years, so it is computed and published in the data but deliberately not drawn as a curve.

The third stage covers soil and pests. Bare-soil days are dry-season days with smoothed NDVI below 0.30, measured per field from the satellite record rather than assumed. Under the current corn-only rotation the demonstration fields sit bare an average of 107 days a year; the corn-brachiaria consortium cuts that to 11, and a crotalaria cover crop to 43. Field studies in Brazil justify this as a degradation indicator: soil and water losses fall sharply with residue cover, with roughly half the runoff at 90% cover compared to bare soil (Bragantia, 2015). Slope from SRTM provides the erosion component, and our eleven fields run from 2.7 to 4.0 degrees. The pest table is built from the regional literature. Off-season Crotalaria spectabilis, alone or with ADR 300 pearl millet, was the most suitable option to reduce Pratylenchus brachyurus populations and soybean damage in trials run in Vera, Mato Grosso, the same region as our demonstration farm (Debiasi et al., 2016, Pesquisa Agropecuaria Brasileira), with suppression confirmed for sole-cropped crotalaria species (Cruz et al., 2020, Ciencia Rural). For the corn leafhopper, the corn-stunt outbreak in Brazil is attributed to overlapping corn seasons that sustain Dalbulus maidis year-round, with annual losses estimated at US$6.5 billion, and breaking that green bridge is listed among the core management measures (Pozebon et al., 2022, Journal of Economic Entomology, doi 10.1093/jee/toac147). Our score therefore penalizes corn after corn and rewards a corn-free season when these pests are flagged. The corn-brachiaria card follows Embrapa trials showing the consortium maintains second-crop corn yield while adding straw, with following-season soybean outyielding soybean grown over sole-corn residue by about 7 sacks per hectare.

The fourth stage is the score: each strategy combines income potential, soil protection and success probability, normalized to a 0-100 scale and weighted by the farmer's slider settings, computed client-side in plain JavaScript. The same scoring runs field by field and is then aggregated area-weighted across the farm, so the tool also answers the question a manager actually asks, one succession crop for all 1,479 hectares, while showing which fields disagree with that choice.

The immediate benefit is a better-timed succession decision: the tool shows each field's real planting window and the historical odds of each option, so the farmer can avoid sowing corn into a window where it fails in most years, or discover that a cover crop fits where a cash crop does not. At Mato Grosso's scale, where millions of hectares make this same call in the same few weeks, even marginal improvements in sowing timing and rotation choice move national production and reduce losses like the US$6.5 billion a year already attributed to the corn leafhopper alone. The longer-term impact is on the soil that sustains the system, and the method generalizes: every input is a public satellite or climate product, so the same pipeline can be run for any rainfed grain region in the world.

The project was developed with Google Earth Engine (JavaScript and Python) for satellite exports, Python with pandas and SciPy for NDVI smoothing, phenology detection, the water balance and the scoring tables, and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet and Tailwind for the site. The site is static, hosted on GitHub Pages, and reads pre-computed JSON tables. There is no server and no build step, so the demo cannot fail from infrastructure. A farmer can also upload their own field boundary as a GeoJSON file and get the same analysis for their own land.

The creative core of the project is that the harvest prediction is not the product but the measuring instrument. Most crop tools predict yield; Field Shift predicts a date, because the date is what converts satellite data into an agronomic decision: how many days of rain remain. A second deliberate choice is honesty as a design feature. Predictions appear as P10, P50 and P90 ranges rather than single dates, every strategy card lists what the data does not cover, a five-year ENSO sample is withheld rather than drawn as a confident curve, and a fixed notice states that the tool supports the farmer's agronomist and does not replace them.

The team considered three main factors. Scope was cut deliberately: one crop system and one region, represented by a demonstration farm of eleven real, rainfed fields totalling 1,479 hectares near Sorriso, in the heart of Mato Grosso's grain belt, so that every number shown could be computed and verified within the event. Results were validated instead of assumed: the harvest model was tested by replaying the 2025/26 season with data frozen in December, its first formulation was rejected on that evidence, and the water balance was accepted only after it reproduced the behavior documented in the agronomic literature cited above. Finally, the user shaped the interface: it is built for a farmer on a phone, in plain language that avoids technical vocabulary except where a tooltip can explain it. The demonstration site is presented in English for the international challenge; a Portuguese version for the Brazilian farmer is the natural first localization.

Regarding the use of super intelligence: the team used Anthropic's Claude as an assistant for coding and for drafting text, always under team direction and review. Parts of the Python pipeline, the JavaScript scoring code and the site were written or reviewed with Claude, recorded in every repository commit's metadata, and the documentation and the text on this page were drafted with Claude and edited by the team. No SI-generated images, video or audio were used, and the tool itself contains no SI component: it is a deterministic pipeline whose every number is reproducible from the open scripts and cited public sources.
